newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Kamajor militia attacks east Sierra Leone town.
newsitem.headline: Kamajor militia attacks east Sierra Leone town.

text.p: Kamajor traditional hunters attacked soldiers loyal to Sierra Leone's military ruler Johnny Paul Koroma in the eastern region capital of Kenema on Thursday, residents and the regional governor said.
The ruling military council accused West African giant Nigeria of arming the Kamajors and a mercenary force to overthrow Koroma and reverse his May 25 coup.
Eastern region governor Captain Eddie Kanneh told Reuters by telephone from Kenema that truck loads of Kamajors, who have refused to rally to the coup, attacked on several fronts.

Residents fleeing the diamond-mining town reported many dead, including civilians. They said by telephone that the fighting began early on Thursday when most people were still in bed but appeared to die down by late afternoon.

"There are so many bodies of Kamajors lying around killed in the battle today between government soldiers and Kamajors for control of Kenema," Kanneh said, adding that soldiers had suffered gunshot wounds and other injuries.
He said the army had driven back the Kamajor attackers and would not let them near the town again.
The attack was the latest in a series of clashes between the Kamajors and the army in the region.
Junior army officers seized power on May 25, toppling civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule.

Kabbah used the Kamajors as a civil militia to help the army push back rebels who took up arms in 1991. The coup leaders accuse him of humiliating the army and blocking peace with the rebels, who rallied to the coup and have flooded into the capital Freetown.

A statement from the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council said former defence minister, Retired Captain Samuel Hinga Norman, had held secret meetings in Liberia with the Nigerian head of the Nigerian-dominated peacekeeping force and other officers.

"Large quantities of arms, ammunition and rations were dished out for his (Norman's) Kamajors, non-Sierra Leonean mercenaries and Nigerian troops backed by batteries of Nigerian artillery," said the statement, read on national radio.
Civilian politicians and Sierra Leone's West African neighbours insist that Kabbah be reinstated, something the coup leaders have rejected.
Nigerian gunboats bombarded the capital Freetown in a show of force on June 2 and dissident soldiers and rebels attacked Nigerian soldiers who were there under a defence accord.
A widely anticipated Nigerian attack has not materialised.
Koroma was sworn in as head of state on Tuesday and pledged to restore peace and eventually democracy to the war-weary West African nation and establish a broad-based government.
Koroma said both the rebel Revolutionary United Front and the Kamajors, who have kept their distance from the coup leaders, would have a place in the government.
Kamajor leaders have said that they will not join a broad- based government and want to stay out of politics.
The United States, France, Lebanon and other nations evacuated their own and other foreign nationals.
Military officials said on Monday they had arrested eight army officers and seven civilians on suspicion of plotting a fresh coup and trying to enlist the support of rebel fighters.
